piknit

A way to embed the Pi coding agent in R. Drive a live agent from R with a small scripting API — pi_run() for one turn, pi_session() for a memory-keeping multi-turn session — or drop it straight into R Markdown / Quarto through knitr engines that run a live agent (and fail-loud shell commands) at render time, weaving the agent’s real replies and command output into the document. Rendering becomes an integration test: a stale claim or a broken command fails the build. Same idea as leanknit and duckknit, pointed at an agent.

Two ways to use it:

  • As an R binding — pi_run() / pi_session() call a Pi agent from any R script, app, or pipeline; the agent (with its tools and extensions) becomes a function you call and whose reply you keep.
  • As literate engines — ```{pi} and ```{pish} chunks put a live agent and fail-loud commands into a rendered document.

Install 

# remotes::install_github("sounkou-bioinfo/piknit")
library(piknit)

Needs the pi CLI on the PATH. Set defaults with options(piknit.model=, piknit.provider=) or the PIKNIT_PI env var.

Call the agent from R

The agent is a function you call; its reply is a character vector you keep — run live when this README renders:

reply <- pi_run("In one sentence, what is a coding agent?")
reply
A coding agent is an AI assistant that can inspect, modify, run, and test code using tool-based actions to autonomously help implement or fix software.

Point it at an extension (extension = "path/to/index.ts") to give the agent tools. That is the whole embedding: pi_run() is one turn, pi_session() is a memory-keeping conversation, and the knitr engines below are just these calls wired into a render.

The pi engine — the chunk body is the prompt

Write a prompt in a ```{pi} chunk; at render time a live agent turn runs and its reply is woven in under the exact command used. A small, fast model (gpt-5.3-codex-spark by default) keeps a live turn to seconds.

```{pi}
In one sentence, what is literate programming?
```
pi --model gpt-5.3-codex-spark -p \
  "In one sentence, what is literate programming?"

Literate programming is a software development style in which you write programs as a human-readable narrative—interleaving explanation and documentation with code so that the program is meant to be read and understood as a piece of literature, not just executed by a machine.

The pish engine — fail-loud shell

Run a command; a non-zero exit stops the render (never bakes a failure as an answer), and JSON output is fenced for highlighting.

```{pish}
node --version
```

Set the project root

pi treats its working directory as the project root — what scopes the agent’s file tools and where relative extension / skill / manifest paths resolve. Point any call at a root with dir:

pi_run(
  "Count variants by consequence in examples/variant-counts/manifest.json.",
  dir = "~/pi-bio-agent",
  extension = "extensions/pi-coding-agent/index.ts"
)

Stream the response

Because pi’s --mode rpc emits JSON events as they happen, pi_stream() delivers the reply incrementally — assistant text as deltas, every event to a callback — ending on pi’s agent_end:

pi_stream("Explain content-addressed storage in two sentences.")          # prints as it is typed
pi_stream("...", on_event = function(ev) if (ev$type == "turn_end") message("done"))

A persistent session across chunks

pi_session() gives successive turns shared conversation memory (via a stable --session-id) without holding a long-lived process, so an earlier chunk’s result is in scope later:

s <- pi_session(dir = "~/pi-bio-agent", extension = "extensions/pi-coding-agent/index.ts")
s$ask("Load examples/variant-counts/manifest.json and count variants by consequence.")
s$ask("Now express the same counts as percentages.")  # remembers the table above

Why

Docs that run don’t drift. Pointing the render at a live agent turns a README, a vignette, or a tutorial into a real end-to-end test of the agent, its tools, and the claims you make about them — the discipline that caught real bugs while building pi-bio-agent, piknit’s first user.
